articles.title: [OPINION] Twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war
articles.summary: The communist party could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, who signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections…

blocks.text: After the split in the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) in 1993, many doubted that the communist insurgency waged by the CPP and its New People’s Army (NPA) would ever recover. But it did, even surpassing the peak armed strength achieved in the 1980s, first in 2005 then again in 2017.
Since then, however, the CPP-NPA, reeling from the government’s intense counter-insurgency operations, has fallen into a slump, in fact, into the most serious crisis in its entire 58-year history.
Is it twilight time for the CPP-NPA insurgency?

From very modest beginnings, the CPP-NPA grew into a powerful nationwide rebel force during the era of President Ferdinand Marcos, Sr. When the NPA launched its Maoist-style “protracted people’s war” in 1969, it started out as a ragtag band of about 60 fighters, nine automatic rifles and 26 single-shot rifles and pistols in Central Luzon. During the period of martial law, the NPA established guerrilla fronts in all of the country’s strategic mountainous areas outside of the Moro areas. NPA guerrillas engaged the Philippine military in tactical offensives, and built up its armed strength.

In the early 1980s, some CPP cadres advocated adjustments to the party’s revolutionary strategy, arguing that its Maoist strategy, which involved “encircling the cities from the countryside” was much too weighted in favor of military over political struggle and rural over urban struggles. They put forward such alternative strategies as the Vietnamese version of “protracted people’s war” which regarded both military and political struggles as fundamental and decisive, and the “insurrectional strategy” of the Sandinistas in Nicaragua, which had asserted the primacy of the “insurrectional mass movement” over the military struggle.

Because of the CPP’s boycott of the 1986 presidential election, the CPP and the open “national democratic” (ND) movement were left out of the “people power” uprising. But apart from being a tactical mistake, the boycott fiasco also showed up the flaw in the CPP-NPA’s revolutionary strategy. While its forces were still struggling to develop its military struggle along the stipulated stages of Mao’s “protracted people’s war,” the Filipino masses had toppled the Marcos dictatorship through an unarmed insurrection.

Peace negotiations between the government of the late president Corazon Aquino and the CPP’s politico-diplomatic arm, the National Democratic Front (NDF) in 1986-87 quickly collapsed. The government had demanded that the CPP-NPA-NDF lay down its arms, while the NDF had insisted that the talks address the roots of the country’s problems. (The NDF conducted peace talks with each of the post-authoritarian administrations, but did not reach a comprehensive political settlement with any of them.)

For a while after the boycott fiasco, the NPA continued to grow, reaching its highest level in 1987. The NPA was widely reported to have swelled to 25,000 fighters, although CPP founding chair Jose Ma. Sison later belied that the NPA ever reached that number in the 1980s. The CPP-NPA measures its armed strength mainly in terms of high-powered rifles (such as M16, M14, AK-47 and M1 Garand). According to Sison, the NPA’s armed strength “increased to 6,100 automatic rifles in 1986 and still further increased by some hundreds in 1987,” its highest level up to that time.

Then the decline started. The political fallout from the boycott fiasco started impacting on the CPP-NPA. This was compounded by the revelations about the killings of hundreds of suspected government spies in the CPP-NPA’s anti-infiltration purges in 1982-89. The fall of the socialist states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union raised questions about the very rectitude of the revolutionary left’s socialist project.

Disagreements within the CPP leadership related to revolutionary strategy, analysis of the contemporary situation, alternative social order, intra-party democracy and other major questions reached a boiling point in the early 1990s. Sison wrote up “Reaffirm Our Basic Principles and Rectify the Errors,” in which he lashed out at those critical of the party’s Maoist tenets, accusing them of propagating a line of “military adventurism” and “insurrectionism.” The CPP split into “reaffirmists” and “rejectionists,” with the “reaffirmists” emerging as the legatee CPP. Through most of the 1990s, the CPP-NPA suffered an ebb.

At the turn of the millennium, however, the CPP-NPA started to recover. NPA guerrilla attacks picked up in many regions. The CPP-NPA intensified its collection of “revolutionary tax” from mining, agribusiness, telecommunications and construction firms, as well as of “permit-to-campaign” fees from politicians campaigning in or near NPA zones during election periods. In 2005, the NPA armed strength, it was claimed, surpassed the earlier 1987 peak by a few hundred high-powered rifles.

Various counterinsurgency measures undertaken during the administration of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, soon took their toll on the CPP-NPA, which then suffered a decline. In 2002, following the 9-11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the CPP and the NPA had been included in the list of “foreign terrorist organizations” (FTOs) of the US, the European Union and Australia. The next year, as government-NDF peace talks seemed to be going nowhere, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo added the CPP-NPA to her government’s counter-terrorist Oplan Bantay Laya, which originally targeted the Abu Sayyaf only. The Oplan strategy combined combat, intelligence and civil-military operations, and emphasized the “neutralization” of communists. Scores of open ND leaders and activists were arrested, tortured, disappeared or summarily executed. In 2006, Arroyo declared an “all-out war” against the CPP-NPA and the extrajudicial killings of leftists worsened. NPA armed strength was said to have dropped by 21.6% over 2006-2009.

Starting in 2010, however, the CPP-NPA recovered again. NPA guerrilla operations intensified all over the country. In Mindanao, where the NPA was strongest, tactical offensives reportedly increased from 250 in 2010, 350 in 2011, 400 in 2012, more than 400 each in 2013 and 2014, and more than 500 in 2015. The NPA’s arena of operations, it was further claimed, expanded to 110 guerrilla fronts in 73 of the country’s 81 provinces. According to Sison, NPA armed strength “surpassed the previous 2005 peak by 3 per cent” – that is, to over 7,000 high-powered rifles.

But storm clouds were brewing. In late 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte adopted a “whole-of-nation” approach in combating the CPP-NDF insurgency, a year after it had terminated peace talks with the NDF. The approach, which sought to mobilize and synchronize civilian government agencies, local government units, and military forces in counterinsurgency efforts, combined barangay development projects (roads, water systems, other infrastructure, schools, health stations and livelihood assistance) with localized peace engagements (including local integration of former rebels) in conflict-affected areas. To implement such a strategy, Duterte created a multi-agency National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), headed by the president himself. President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. continued Duterte’s “whole-of-nation” approach.

From the government’s viewpoint, the “whole-of-nation” strategy has been a tremendous success. In 2024, Marcos claimed that no NPA guerrilla fronts remained active across the country. The NTF-ELCAC added that the NPA had been reduced to only 785 “remnants.” In the light of many reports of clashes between the military and the NPA over the last two years, the government’s exultant claims are not credible.

But the CPP-NPA has indeed suffered grave setbacks. Since the launching of the “whole-of-nation” approach, NPA numbers have dropped considerably, and guerrilla attacks have declined. The International Crisis Group (ICG) estimates that the NPA has shrunk to between 1,200 and 2,000 fighters. The CPP-NPA no longer provides figures of NPA tactical offensives, but the number of clashes between government forces and Red fighters are indicative of the CPP-NPA’s decline. According to the international NGO Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), only 106 clashes occurred between government forces and the NPA in 2025 versus 273 in 2020 – a 61% decline in five years. Mindanao, as a whole, is no longer the main NPA flash point. The main areas of armed encounters have shifted from Western Visayas and Northern Mindanao to Eastern Visayas and Caraga.

blocks.caption: [OPINION] How the Philippine Left lost its way

blocks.text: Over the past eight years, many top CPP-NPA leaders have been killed by the military – in combat or through summary execution. Among them are CPP chairman Benito Tiamzon and secretary-general Wilma Tiamzon, as well as Julius Giron, Antonio Cabanatan, Jorge Madlos, Menandro Villanueva, Maria Concepcion Araneta, Eugenia Magpantay, Randall Echanis and Mariano Adlao. Some other top leaders, such as Victor Ladlad and Rey Casambre. have been arrested and incarcerated.

The Philippines’ “all-of-nation” approach has been widely criticized for thousands of human rights violations – illegal arrests, detentions, torture, extrajudicial killings and disappearances. Many open, legal progressive activists have become easy targets of government harassment and repression. Obsessed with its counterinsurgency drive, the government has largely ignored the criticisms and denunciations of human rights groups.
According to the ICG, the CPP-NPA is at its lowest ebb in decades. Will it be able to recover as it has in the past?

One factor that will make recovery difficult is that the CPP-NPA has lost many of its most experienced leaders over the past eight years or so. Apart from top leaders killed or arrested and imprisoned by the military, some senior, long-serving leaders have passed away peacefully, among them Sison himself, Jose Luneta, Fidel Agcaoili and Luis Jalandoni. A few other veterans have been incapacitated by health problems. The loss of the likes of Sison, Jalandoni and Madlos has also left a big gap in the CPP-NPA’s public-facing spokespersons.

The CPP-NPA may partially recover for a while, but one thing is definite: it will never be able to achieve the total military victory that it has long aspired for. Its fundamental Maoist principles stipulate that before the revolutionary forces can triumph, the “protracted people’s war” has to progress from guerrilla warfare to regular mobile warfare and eventually to positional warfare; and from strategic defensive to strategic stalemate and eventually to strategic offensive. All through nearly six decades of fighting, the NPA has been stuck in guerrilla warfare and the strategic defensive.

Endeavoring to extricate the CPP-NPA from its guerrilla warfare rut, NPA chieftain Romulo Kintanar had pushed for the establishment of bigger NPA formations and for “regularization” in the 1980s. Sison accused him of “military adventurism” and had him expelled from the CPP-NPA, then assassinated. Kintanar had established extensive international linkages for the NPA, knowing that only external sources could provide a sizeable and steady supply of arms and ammunition needed for moving up to regular warfare. This international network withered away after the takeover of the NPA by the “reaffirmist” CPP leadership. (It must be noted here that the Moro National Liberation Front and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, during their wars for secession, did manage to secure arms from external sources, but still did not achieve military victory against the government.)

The CPP-NPA’s “protracted people’s war” has gone on much longer than any of America’s “forever wars.” As defined by Cambridge Dictionary, a forever war is “a war that never ends because it cannot be won.” It is a prolonged, open-ended armed conflict without a clear, achievable endpoint or decisive victory. The war without end between the government and the CPP-NPA has already claimed between 40,000 to 60,000 lives. Yet, each year, on the NPA’s anniversary on March 29, it celebrates the protraction of its “people’s war.”

It’s twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war. Mao’s rural and peasant-based “protracted people’s war,” employed in “semicolonial, semifeudal” China a century ago, simply has been a bad fit for an urbanizing Philippine society with a middle income economy that has shifted away from agriculture and is increasingly dominated by wage labor and the service sector.

Communist insurgencies are on the wane worldwide. The CPP-NPA insurgency is one of a handful of major communist insurgencies still surviving in the contemporary world. Two of them, both Maoist, have not fared any better than the CPP-NPA. India’s Naxalites (Communist Party of India – Maoist), who have waged a 59-year-old “people’s war,” are dwindling, reduced to isolated pockets and struggling with recruitment and funding, with a leadership severely degraded. Peru’s Shining Path (Communist Party of Peru), whose founder, Abimael Guzman, was captured in 1992 and died in prison in 2021, has been all but dismantled, with a few splinter groups financing themselves mainly through cocaine trafficking.

If the CPP still hopes to come to power, it should work out a comprehensive political settlement with the government and strive to turn its still appreciable mass base into an electoral base. All of the government-NDF peace negotiations have come to naught. The CPP-NPA-NDF has only been interested in eking out tactical gains – propaganda, release of political prisoners, immunity for “NDF negotiators,” so-called “belligerency status” – while still obdurately aiming for total military victory. Protracted negotiations was merely a tactic in its “protracted people’s war.”

The CPP could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist, now Maoist Centre), which signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections in 2008–2009 and has been in the ruling coalition several times since then.

Back in 1991, writing under the pseudonym Omar Tupaz, I commented on the CPP-NPA’s Maoist “protracted people’s war” strategy: “It will be difficult, if not impossible, to win a revolution in the 1990s by continuing to adhere to a basic strategic framework of a bygone era.” Unfortunately for the CPP-NPA, this seems to be coming to pass. – Rappler.com

Nathan Gilbert Quimpo authored Contested Democracy and the Left after Marcos and co-authored Subversive Lives: A Family Memoir of the Marcos Years. In the 1980s and 1990s, he penned critiques of the communist party’s revolutionary strategy under the pseudonym Marty Villalobos and Omar Tupaz.

articles.title: What are the powers of the Supreme Court, responsibilities of the chief justice?
articles.summary: The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has concluded its interviews for the position of Supreme Court (SC) chief justice, which will be vacated by Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo in November.

blocks.text: The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has concluded its interviews for the position of Supreme Court (SC) chief justice, which will be vacated by Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo in November.
The next chief justice will lead the country’s highest court and oversee the administration of the Judiciary, while helping ensure that the Supreme Court fulfills its constitutional mandate.
Under the 1987 Constitution, what are the powers of the Supreme Court and the responsibilities of the chief justice?
Powers of the Supreme Court
The Supreme Court is composed of the chief justice and 14 associate justices. It may sit en banc, or as a full court, or in divisions of three, five or seven justices.
Article VIII, Section 5 of the Constitution enumerates the powers of the Supreme Court, including the following:
1. Decide cases involving constitutional questions.

The SC reviews cases involving the constitutionality or validity of laws, treaties, international or executive agreements, presidential decrees, proclamations, orders, instructions, ordinances and regulations.

It may also review cases involving the legality of taxes and penalties, questions concerning the jurisdiction of lower courts, criminal cases in which the penalty imposed is reclusion perpetua or higher, and cases involving questions of law.
2. Hear certain cases in the first instance.

The Court exercises original jurisdiction over cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, as well as petitions for certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto and habeas corpus.

These legal remedies allow the Court, under applicable rules, to address issues such as alleged jurisdictional errors, unlawful exercises of authority, challenges to a person's entitlement to public office and unlawful detention.
3. Issue rules governing court proceedings and the legal profession.

The SC may promulgate rules on the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, court pleadings and procedures, admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar and legal assistance for underprivileged people.
These rules must promote simplified, inexpensive and speedy court proceedings and must not diminish, increase or modify substantive rights.
4. Exercise administrative powers over the Judiciary.
Under Article VIII, Section 6, the SC exercises administrative supervision over all courts and their personnel.

The Constitution also authorizes the Court to appoint Judiciary officials and employees in accordance with civil service law, temporarily assign lower court judges to other stations when public interest requires, and order changes of venue or place of trial to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
The SC en banc may also discipline lower court judges or order their dismissal, subject to the constitutional voting requirements.
Responsibilities of the chief justice

The chief justice heads the Supreme Court but does not exercise all its powers independently. Decisions on cases are made by the Court, sitting en banc or in divisions, in accordance with the Constitution and applicable rules.
The chief justice has several specific responsibilities.
1. Preside over the Supreme Court.
As head of the Court, the chief justice presides over its proceedings, including sessions of the SC en banc.
2. Certify compliance with the consultation requirement.

Article VIII, Section 13 requires the conclusions of the Court in cases submitted for decision, whether en banc or in division, to be reached in consultation before a case is assigned to a member for the writing of the Court's opinion.
The chief justice must sign a certification that this requirement has been met. A copy must be attached to the case record and served on the parties.
3. Lead the Judiciary's administration.

The chief justice heads the institution responsible for administering justice through the Supreme Court and the lower courts. The Court's administrative supervision covers all courts and their personnel.
The chief justice's leadership therefore includes overseeing the Judiciary's administration and helping ensure that the courts carry out their constitutional and legal responsibilities.
4. Chair the Judicial and Bar Council.
Under Article VIII, Section 8, the chief justice serves as the ex officio chairperson of the JBC, the body primarily responsible for recommending appointees to the Judiciary.

The JBC prepares a list of at least three nominees for every judicial vacancy, from which the President appoints members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts, subject to the Constitution's provisions.
5. Uphold judicial independence and accountability.
The chief justice, like other members of the Judiciary, must meet the constitutional standards of competence, integrity, probity and independence.

Under Article VIII, Section 11, Supreme Court justices and lower court judges generally hold office during good behavior until they reach 70 years old or become incapacitated to discharge their duties.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Netherlands makes U-turn over Eurovision return
articles.summary: A Dutch broadcaster reverses a decision to take part, citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation.

blocks.text: NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.
"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.
"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."
NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".
Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.
"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."
Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

articles.title: DR Congo reports over 10,000 Ebola cases as the outbreak spreads abroad, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus
articles.summary: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain…

image.caption: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases in what Africa CDC calls the fastest-growing outbreak in history (FILE 22/10/2026)Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

blocks.text: Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Where else have cases been reported?
Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.
Nigeria on alert after traveler tests positive for Ebola
Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.
Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.
The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.

articles.title: ‘I’m still innocent,’ says Comey as Trump calls him a ‘dirty cop’ – US politics live
articles.summary: The US justice department is attempting to prosecute the former FBI director for the third time

blocks.text: ‘I’m still innocent,’ says Comey as Trump calls him a ‘dirty cop’
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump has called the former FBI director, James Comey, a “dirty cop”, Reuters reports. The US justice department is attempting to prosecute Comey for a third time, on the grounds of sharing sensitive national security information in ⁠2016, according to court documents ⁠made public on Monday.

The case was revealed in a court document known as a “criminal information” that the justice department said ⁠it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.

The document, filed in Washington federal ⁠court, charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from ‌the New York Times ‌in October 2016.
“I think he’s a dirty cop,” president Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, when asked about Comey. “I don’t know much about ‌it,” he said.

Comey said in a video on Instagram that “they’re back again” and ‌referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. “I’m still innocent,” he added. Comey’s lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump campaigned in Corinth, Mississippi in support of Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and told the crowd his rallies have “totally changed the dialogue”. “Nobody’s ever campaigned like I have for midterms,” he said.
A vocal protester then attempted to engage the president in some dialogue, on the subject of his ballroom, and where it might be most appropriately located.

Trump lashed out in racist terms at his predecessor, Barack Obama, for joking over the weekend that his renovation of the White House, with “gold everywhere”, has “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein open a Cheesecake Factory.”

Trump told reporters that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” of the White House before he rehabilitated it. Trump said then that he was “a very clean person” but, “you have to explain that to Obama” because the former president doesn’t understand and is “not smart at all.”
Trump said that the comeback victory of Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, “looked like another rigged election, frankly.”

Social media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood of AI-driven disinformation ahead of November’s US midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are likely “slipping through the cracks”.
As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.

While the backlash against Facebook after the Cambridge Analytica scandal prompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election of Donald Trump in 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.
Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.

“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in Big Tech. Operatives playing dirty tricks can get around content moderation rules “because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through”, she said.

President Donald Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday plan to show off a newly arrived oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude to be processed in Texas refineries, according to a congressional aide and two US officials.
The visit to Port Arthur, Texas, comes on the same day that Trump is campaigning in the state for Republican candidates in the midterms, AP reported.

The president has rallies scheduled in Corpus Christi and Lubbock. Trump is trying to shore up support for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a tight race with Democratic candidate James Talarico.

It’s not clear whether Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser, would take part in any campaign events. But it’s the first time that he’s hitting the road with Trump as the president barnstorms the country.
The two US officials and the congressional aide spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss Rubio’s plans before they were publicly announced.

It’s highly unusual for the nation’s top diplomat to participate in political travel. Rubio’s trip would be the latest example of how Trump’s second presidency has blurred the lines between governing and campaigning. Attorney-general Todd Blanche has already been appearing at rallies alongside Republican candidates.

Rubio previously ran for president in 2016 and is considered a top prospect in 2028. He has not said whether he will run, and his political activities have been limited since becoming secretary of state.

articles.title: Who is Retrina Fuentes, the judge behind arrest orders vs Duterte critics?
articles.summary: Fuentes once served as executive judge of the Davao City Regional Trial Court

items: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyber libel case filed by lawyer Mans Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Lustre was detained for nearly a day before posting bail and is known for his book on extrajudicial killings in the Philippines, while he plans to release a new book amid the Vice President's impeachment trial.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on Saturday, October 24, over a cyber libel case filed by an unidentified complainant at the time. It was Davao City Presiding Judge Retrina Espe Fuentes who issued the warrant of arrest.
On Monday, October 26, Lustre’s lawyer, Dino de Leon, told Rappler that it was lawyer Mans Carpio — husband of Vice President Sara Duterte — who was the complainant in Lustre’s case.

Based on the Supreme Court’s (SC) tracker, Fuentes is currently the presiding judge of Davao City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10. The court is located in Benigno Aquino Hall of Justice, in Matina, Davao City.
Fuentes was Davao City’s 1st vice executive judge in 2016, according to the Philippine Judicial Academy Bulletin. At the time, Presiding Judge Emmanuel Carpio was sitting as executive judge.
Presiding Judge Carpio is the uncle of Mans Carpio. In her 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, Vice President Duterte listed Emmanuel Carpio as her uncle-in-law.
At the time of Fuentes’ appointment as 1st vice executive judge, Rodrigo Duterte was president, while his daughter Sara was Davao City mayor during that period.
Based on SC Office of the Court Administrator’s Administrative Order No. 231-2022, Fuentes became Davao City’s executive judge on November 1, 2022 under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

The Fraternal Order of Saint Thomas More in Davao City posted a congratulatory message after Fuentes’ appointment. She held the position from 2022 to 2024, according to SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting.
“Davao Regional Trial Court Executive Judge is now Judge Rowena M. Apao Adlawan,” said Ting.

According to the SC’s AM No. 03-8-02-SC, the Court may appoint executive judges and vice executive judges in stations where there are more than two RTC branches. Their appointment will be based on their administrative qualifications, experience, and seniority, among others.

“The Executive Judge shall take charge of the administrative work of the Supreme Court in all first and second level courts. The Executive Judge derives his/her powers and prerogatives through delegation by the Supreme Court,” said the order.
Lustre, the 72-year-old veteran journalist was attending the Saturday News Forum event in Quezon City when Quezon City police from the Quezon City Police District arrested him.
After nearly a day in detention, he was able to post a P48,000-bail at past midnight on Sunday, October 25.

Lustre is the author of the book, “Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines.” It’s about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights groups. Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands over his crimes against humanity case that stemmed from the said campaign.

After his release from temporary detention, Lustre said he is scheduled to release a new book titled, “MISFIT SARA Life and Times of Vice President Sara Duterte-Carpio; The Impeachment Trial of a Filipino Vice President.” The Vice President is currently in the middle of her impeachment trial that could remove her from the position and bar her from running for president in 2028.

The information sheet against Lustre reads: “The above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account under the name ‘Philip Jr. Lustre,’ published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Manases R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called ‘Facebook.com,’ by saying: ‘Sumuka si Mans Carpio ng P300-M sa operasyon ng Marines: P150M kay Mike; P50M kay Levi; at P5M sa bawat isa sa 18 Marines?‘ which published statement, taken in its plain, natural, and ordinary meaning, directly imputes upon Atty. Manases R. Carpio, the commission of a crime, specifically bribery or corrupt.”

blocks.caption: Philip Lustre Jr.’s arrest a ‘warning’ for journalists – lawyer

blocks.text: Fuentes was also the judge who signed the warrant of arrest against another Duterte critic and former vice presidential candidate, Walden Bello.

In 2022, at the height of the campaign season, former Davao City public information officer Jefry Tupas filed a cyber libel complaint against Bello. Tupas was seeking P10 million in damages after being allegedly accused by Bello on social media of being a drug addict and dealer.

Duterte’s aide was embroiled in a controversy in 2021 after attending a beach party in Mabini, Davao de Oro that was later raided by anti-narcotics agents. The operation supposedly happened an hour after Tupas and companions had left the party.
On August 8, 2022, QCPD personnel arrested Bello over a warrant issued by Fuentes for two counts of cyber libel. He was later freed after posting a P48,000-bail for each of the counts.
Bello, at the time, labeled Tupas’ case as “clearly a politically-motivated move.”
The following year, Bello filed a petition with the SC seeking to decriminalize libel in the Philippines.
In February this year, the former vice presidential bet issued an apology to Tupas, saying his statements were “unfounded.”

In 2019, Fuentes was the judge who ordered the arrest of Italian Lorenzo Marchesi, who was 57 years old at the time. He was ordered arrested over alleged possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation materials.
Marchesi was arrested after a search of his electronic devices allegedly revealed a collection of illegal materials.
Last September, Fuentes was the same judge who issued a warrant of arrest against a man wanted for rape. She issued the warrant on September 2, 2026.

“The accused, identified only by the alias ‘Abdul,’ was properly informed of the cause of his arrest and apprised of his constitutional rights, including his rights under Republic Act No. 9745, or the Anti-Torture Act of 2009, in a language or dialect known to and understood by him,” said the PNP.
“The arrested person was identified as a top 3 most wanted person, municipal level, under the PNP e-warrant system,” it added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Parks Canada ends search and rescue dog program
articles.summary: Parks Canada has quietly axed a search and rescue dog program that dates back to the early 1970s. It was highly used in the mountain national parks for backcountry rescues, to search for missing…

image.caption: A scene above slidepaths in Corral Creek in Banff National Park with Parks Canada search and rescue dog Attila. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)

blocks.text: Calgary

Parks Canada has quietly axed a search and rescue dog program that dates back to the early 1970s. It was highly used in the mountain national parks for backcountry rescues, to search for missing people, support local police, locate people who died in avalanches and find illegal campsites.
2025 federal budget includes $145M in cuts to Parks Canada over 3 years
Parks Canada has quietly axed a search and rescue dog program that dates back to the early 1970s.
“It’s a really big service to visitor safety and law enforcement,” said Scott Ward, a retired Parks Canada dog handler, who worked as a warden for 35 years and a handler from 1983 to 2000.
“It’s getting busier every year. The calls are going up. The visitor safety people are way busier now than they were in my era.”
Mike Henderson, a dog handler in Banff National Park from 2001-19, said he understands the need to save money, but cutting the canine program could reduce safety.

“You’re cutting a piece that’s not obsolete. It’s got 55 years of success, and we keep on proving ourselves. … It’s not like we sat on our laurels or were hyper expensive at any time,” said Henderson, who had three dogs — Attila, Atar and Cazz — and was involved in more than 1,000 calls.

items: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union

blocks.text: The last search and rescue dog, Leroy, was retired last summer after a seven-year career. Leroy was involved in finding more than 50 people in the wilderness, located avalanche victims, recovered mountain fatalities, helped stop poaching and was a prominent public relations figure.
Henderson and Ward said a new dog went through about two and a half months of training to be brought into federal service only to have it cut.
The 2025 federal budget included $145 million in cuts to Parks Canada over three years.
A Parks Canada spokesperson said they would get back to CBC News on questions about why the dog program was cut, but didn’t provide an answer before publishing.
Cazz, a Parks Canada search and rescue dog, stands outside an illegal campsite on the edges of the Town of Banff. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)
'Why'd we get rid of it now?'
The search and rescue program was approved in 1970 and started in Jasper National Park.
It was highly used in the mountain national parks for backcountry rescues, to search for missing people, support local police, locate people who died in avalanches and find illegal campsites.
The program grew to six dogs, but was slowly whittled down. The Jasper field unit stopped using dogs more than a decade ago, leaving only Banff.

items: Parks Canada not laying charges after Banff National Park superintendent admits to violating federal law

blocks.text: Sid Marty was a warden in Banff, Jasper and Yoho national parks from 1966-78. He said they worked closely with the search and rescue dog and its handler.
He said the dog could quickly find people caught in avalanches, helping to avoid Parks Canada staff getting caught in subsequent avalanches during a lengthy search.
Search and rescue dog Atar scopes out the scene of a collision involving multiple semi-trucks on the Trans-Canada Highway. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)
Ward said his dogs — Data, Smokey and Gypsy — were critical in finding missing people, such as kids who wandered away from campsites.
He said they were trained to search for human scent “as small as a paperclip in the grass to as large as a human body.”

items: Rescues in the Rockies cost millions each year. Who pays for them?

blocks.text: Henderson emphasized the dogs went beyond search and rescue.

He said their day-to-day could have them handling illegal camping, responding to mental health calls, dealing with illegal campfires, monitoring area closures, removing food to avoid wildlife becoming habituated to it, and monitoring for poaching.
“You can put the rowdy campers to bed,” he said. “You roll in, ask nicely and light the dog up, and everyone says, ‘OK, we’re going to bed.’”

items: Woman fined after grizzly bear run-in with off-leash dog in Banff National Park

blocks.text: Henderson said consultation should’ve taken place to get a better understanding of what would be lost by cutting the program.
“Why'd we get rid of it now? It definitely needs to be spoken to,” Henderson said.
Former Parks Canada warden Mike Henderson and his search and rescue dog in Grasslands National Park in Saskatchewan during an anti-poaching operation. (Submitted by Mike Henderson)
Not only dogs getting the boot

Parks Canada is undergoing a “workforce adjustment” and recently notified 2,917 employees — more than half of its staff — they could be fired or moved to different positions. Andrew Campbell, acting CEO of Parks Canada, said in an all-staff email the federal agency has to cut about 500 full-time jobs.
The full rollout of the new plan is anticipated in 2027, and Campbell said they’re allowing people to voluntarily leave or retire to reduce the number of people who are cut.
“Parks Canada has used, and will continue to use, every tool at its disposal to minimize involuntary departures,” he said in a call to staff.

Greg Colgan is a journalist for CBC in the Bow Valley. He was previously the editor of the Rocky Mountain Outlook in Banff and Canmore. He has also worked for media outlets in Ontario and has experience covering topics such as sports, politics, housing and development, courts and arts and entertainment. He joined CBC in 2025. He can be reached at greg.colgan@cbc.ca.

articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he would remain focused on the impeachment trial amid the call of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to reject offers to succeed Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he would remain focused on the impeachment trial amid the call of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to reject offers to succeed Vice President Sara Duterte should she be convicted.
Gatchalian said a lot is still expected to unfold in the impeachment trial as Duterte’s defense team has yet to present its evidence.
“To be fair sa respondent, hindi pa nape-present ng defense ‘yung kanilang ebidensya at testimony. So pakinggan muna natin lahat bago tayo mag-isip ng next steps,” the Senate President said.
(To be fair to the respondent, the defense has yet to present their evidence and testimony. So let’s hear everything first before we consider the next steps.)
Asked if Gatchalian has received any initial offers for the vice presidency, he said, “Ako, impeachment muna ang tinututukan ko eh.”
(My focus is only on impeachment as of the moment)

“Pinag-aaralan namin mabuti, pinag-aaralan ko mabuti. And of course, ‘yung impeachment proceedings, pinag-aaralan din namin mabuti ‘yung dates, ‘yung times. In the next few days, budget season, papasok na sa plenary. So, ito lahat inaayos namin. So, naka-concentrate muna kami sa process,” he added.

(We are studying this carefully, I am studying it carefully. We are also carefully reviewing the impeachment proceedings’ dates and the schedule. In the next few days, the budget will reach the plenary. We are currently organizing all of this now. So we’re only focusing on the process.)
Cayetano earlier called on his fellow senators to declare that they will decline offers for the vice presidency should Duterte get convicted in her impeachment trial.

The Senate Minority Leader made the appeal in response to the statement of Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero---presiding officer of the impeachment court---that he will refuse the vice presidency, if Duterte gets convicted, due to conflict of interest.
Timeline

Gatchalian also said the impeachment trial may extend up to December given that the Senate has to balance it with the ongoing budget deliberations and the upcoming bicameral conference committee meetings to consolidate disagreeing provisions of the budget bill.
“Parang hindi na kaya ng November from the looks of it. So, I'm sure, tingin ko, tatawid ito ng December,” he said.
(It looks like the impeachment trial can’t conclude by November. So I’m sure it will extend to December.)

The impeachment trial is currently suspended to pave the way for the committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget. The Senate impeachment court shall reconvene on November 9 at 10 a.m. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Make LGU funds ‘results-based’ amid pork barrel concerns — World Bank
articles.summary: “We believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” World Bank lead urban specialist Makiko Watanabe says

blocks.text: “We believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” World Bank lead urban specialist Makiko Watanabe says

MANILA, Philippines – The World Bank said the proposed P58-billion Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget could help power regional development, but recommended tying allocations to actual project results and encouraging local governments to invest together, amid concerns the fund could become a source of political patronage.

Makiko Watanabe, the World Bank’s lead urban specialist for East Asia and the Pacific, said the Philippine government could adopt performance-based or results-based financing to improve accountability and reward local government units (LGUs) that deliver.

“The short answer is, yes, we believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” Watanabe said when asked by Rappler during the launch of the World Bank’s From Cities to Corridors report on Tuesday, October 27.
She suggested that allocations be made “performance-based or results-based” rather than set in advance, and that funding encourage “inter-LGU type of investments” rather than isolated projects.
These could include shared transportation and digital infrastructure, as well as disaster resilience projects that have spillover benefits beyond a single municipality or city.

World Bank Philippines division director Zafer Mustafaoğlu likewise emphasized the need for accountability, efficient spending, and timely project completion, while suggesting too that authorities should consider the economic potential of neighboring LGUs when allocating resources.

The proposed LGSF has drawn scrutiny over concerns that it could be used for discretionary spending and political patronage. Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has questioned the criteria for distributing the more-than-P58-billion fund and called for safeguards to ensure that allocations address local development needs rather than reward political allies. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also said that the LGSF needed to be transparent to promote good governance.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] The 2027 budget: Hocus-pocus prevails once more

blocks.text: The World Bank’s latest report also identifies weaknesses in how local projects secure funding.

Only about 30% of investment proposals endorsed through regional development councils receive funding in a given budget cycle, which may create “uncertainties among LGUs about which of their endorsed priorities will receive the national government support,” the World Bank report said.
It also notes that projects outside local annual investment plans (AIP) can receive funding when they have political backing, while planned projects may go unfunded.

“While AIP is a standard vehicle for investment planning, [focus group discussion] shows that projects are also budgeted outside the AIP when there is political support, whereas AIP-listed items go unfunded when local priorities do not align,” the World Bank said in its report.

blocks.caption: SITTING ON CASH? A World Bank analysis of 2023 year-end cash balance as a share of annual operating revenues by urban LGU size shows that LGUs are not utilizing large amounts of cash on hand. Chart from the World Bank’s report

blocks.text: Beyond the allocation process, many LGUs struggle to spend the funds they already have. Capital investments account for only about 15% of annual LGU expenditure, while poor project preparation and procurement add to delays.

This has left local governments sitting on cash reserves, with large urban LGUs holding an average of P9,263 per person in year-end cash on hand balances in 2023, funds that the World Bank said could have been better used to address infrastructure and service needs.

The report’s main recommendation is to shift away from individual LGU support to what it calls interconnected “corridor-based” development, with aligned national and local plans and better project implementation capacity. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Employees cannot be forced to retire early without consent, Supreme Court says
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employees cannot be retired before the compulsory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 6:05pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employees cannot be retired before the compulsory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent.
In a 22-page decision, the SC’s First Division affirmed that under the Labor Code, an employee may opt to retire upon reaching 60 years old, but compulsory retirement remains set at 65.

“The Labor Code permits employers and employees to fix the applicable retirement age at below 60 years. Absent such an agreement, the retirement age shall be that fixed by law, and the above-cited law mandates that the compulsory retirement age is 65 years, while the minimum age for optional retirement is set at 60 years,” the SC said.

According to court records, petitioner Rodolfo C. Ondevilla was illegally dismissed by his employer, Colegio de San Juan de Letran - Laguna, when his appointment was treated as expired after he turned 60 years old.
The Labor Arbiter and the National Labor Relations Commission both ruled in Ondevilla’s favor, and the Court of Appeals (CA) likewise affirmed that he was illegally dismissed.

While the CA noted that Ondevilla had agreed to retire effective July 31, 2020, based on a letter sent to his employer, the high court affirmed his illegal dismissal because the school had denied his preferred retirement terms.

The SC emphasized that an optional retirement plan must be grounded on a mutual and voluntary agreement, with the employee freely and expressly consenting without pressure or coercion, as accepting optional retirement entails waiving the right to security of tenure.
“Considering that CSJL denied Ondevilla's preference to retire on July 31, 2020, he is deemed to have been illegally dismissed from employment,” the court said.

The Colegio de San Juan de Letran - Laguna was then ordered to pay Ondevilla full backwages from August 29, 2019 until August 29, 2024. He was also declared entitled to separation pay instead of reinstatement.
Furthermore, the SC awarded him retirement benefits covering his period of employment from June 16, 2004, until August 29, 2024, when he reached the mandatory retirement age of 65.
“The total monetary award shall earn legal interest at the rate of 6% per annum from August 29, 2019 until fully paid,” the decision read.
The decision was penned by Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando and promulgated in June 2026 and posted on social media on October 27, 2026. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Yukon photographer captures footage of caribou carrying dead rival in its antlers
articles.summary: WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife. Wildlife photographer Peter Mather said he was “shocked” to find a pair of bull caribou with antlers locked together, one of them dead, in the…

image.caption: In early October, photographer Peter Mather captured a bull caribou with his antlers locked with another, dead bull caribou south of Whitehorse. (Submitted by Peter Mather)

blocks.text: North

WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife. Wildlife photographer Peter Mather said he was “shocked” to find a pair of bull caribou with antlers locked together, one of them dead, in the mountains south of Whitehorse earlier this month. He captured what happened as other wildlife fed off the carcass, still attached to the other bull.
Peter Mather was filming caribou rut south of Whitehorse when he found them
WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife.
Earlier this month, Yukon-based wildlife photographer Peter Mather was on assignment south of Whitehorse to film caribou when he noticed a bear acting unusually aggressive.
“It was huffing and puffing and making noises and we had to scare it off,” Mather said.
Then, another bear came through.
Yukon photographer captures caribou carrying remains after antler entanglement
“When I saw that second bear there, I’m like ‘Oh, there’s probably some sort of dead caribou up there’,” Mather said.
He sent a drone up to see what was happening.
“I was just shocked to see … there’s two caribou with their antlers locked together, and one of them is dead,” he said.
He said he watched a bear nearby try to attack the caribou, but the surviving bull would scare the bear off.
Mather captured a variety of wildlife as they fed on the carcass of the dead bull caribou. Here, a bear and a conspiracy of ravens are seen. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
Mather said he watched this bull caribou for days.
“Over the four days that [dead] caribou disappeared,” Mather said.
“There were foxes … ravens, golden eagles were eating it for four days."
He said on the last day, a pack of wolves arrived at the scene. He believes they got much of the last of the carcass.
“In some ways, [they] kind of freed up this other caribou who could kind of walk away at the end, with two heads,” Mather said.
At one point, a fox stopped by for a meal from the dead caribou. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
Locking antlers not unheard of
Mather said after the wolves arrived and feasted, the living caribou disappeared, and he couldn’t find it.
His work was to record the rut, mating season for caribou that often involve the males fighting one another, with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Team and the Kwanlin Dün First Nation.
Lars Jessup, a biologist with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Project, said this incident happened in a season where bull caribou are especially vulnerable.
“The rut season is the most dangerous time of year for bull caribou … they work really hard in the rut and the predators are usually around during the rut.”
He said bulls locking antlers is somewhat common, describing finding skulls and skeletons of caribou with locked antlers in the past.
“It’s probably more common that when that happens that they both die, not that one of them would live,” Jessup said, calling the living caribou “lucky.”
His time with the extra weight is also coming to an end, Jessup said.
“If he makes it another month or so, he’s likely to drop those antlers and lose the extra weight, and should be fine through winter,” Jessup said.
“By the time people usually see them down the mountains in and around Christmas time … the bulls are usually bald.”
Eventually, other animals managed to free the surviving caribou from having to carry the extra weight of another bull. (Submitted by Peter Mather)
A metaphor for the herd's resiliency
This particular caribou is part of the Ibex herd, Jessup said, one of four caribou herds that make up the southern lakes caribou herds.
It is protected by the southern lakes caribou recovery project, which has continued for more than 30 years.
“The herds have done really well to recover over the last three decades, through all kinds of hard work and effort,” Jessup said.
However, he said there were concerns the natural ebb and flow of the caribou population was in an ebb, as they haven’t seen many calves in the last five years.
For Mather, the photographer, the footage he captured of that one caribou surviving, gives him some hope.
“For me, it’s like a metaphor for the whole herd, that he’s just resilient, just a really, really resilient caribou.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Julia Parrish is a digital associate producer at CBC North in Yellowknife. You can reach her at julia.parrish@cbc.ca
With files from Leonard Linklater

articles.summary: A majority of provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hoped to sweep her nine referendum questions on immigration and constitutional reform, but voters had different ideas, rejecting four of her ballot measures. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
A majority of provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions.
Most provincial ridings rejected most of Danielle Smith's ballot questions
The “strong mandates” that Premier Danielle Smith requested on her nine referendum questions never materialized.
But aside from soft support, there might be another reason Smith is expressing reluctance to act quickly, even on the immigration questions where she won a majority.
Consider that Smith’s own government mandate isn’t derived from the popular vote — it’s based on prevailing in a majority of Alberta’s 87 seats.
And sifting through the riding results from all the referendum questions, some apparent political signals emerge.
Here are some takeaways:
Ridings say no to seven of nine

Smith has signalled she’ll act most quickly on the ballot measure that got the most support — Question 5, to require proof of Canadian citizenship when voting in provincial elections (58 per cent support).
She’s also intent to continue wresting from Ottawa more provincial control over immigration to Alberta, as Question 1 suggested (55 per cent support).

The victory margins were tighter on Questions 2, 3 and 4, to variously restrict social services and financial supports for temporary residents. But on each of those questions, a slight majority of ridings went no — meaning that while four of Smith’s questions failed in terms of total vote, seven of nine would have lost if this was a riding-by-riding contest.
Edmonton was almost uniformly opposed to those temporary resident questions, and only six Calgary ridings were supportive of them.

Twelve Calgary ridings had gone UCP in the last election, which suggests that several parts of Calgary that supported Smith in the 2023 election weren’t on board with her ideas on who should or shouldn’t get fully covered health and education.
Constitutionally blocked
The per-riding results on Question 1 (48 yes, 39 no) roughly tracked the seat math after the last provincial election (48 UCP, 39 NDP).
But on Questions 6 to 9, Smith would have been on the wrong end of the sort of landslides that former premiers Ralph Klein and Jason Kenney enjoyed, had this referendum been settled riding by riding.

More than two-thirds of ridings voted no to Question 8 on opting out of federal social service programs, the most lopsided of the constitutional ballot measures. But in all of them, no was the popular choice in more than 50 constituencies.
Not a single riding in Edmonton or Calgary said yes to a single one of the constitutional questions.
Rural Alberta, however, stayed loyal to Smith’s push for more provincial powers and to tilt Canada’s Constitution in favour of Alberta.
Blue wall, orange wall
Premier Smith asked voters to vote yes on all nine questions that didn’t threaten national unity; NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was effectively part of the “no to the nine” campaign.
According to Elections Alberta, 24 ridings voted no down the line, while 27 voted yes to all of them.

items: Alberta referendum tallies reveal rural-urban divide on ‘the 9’

blocks.text: What went all the UCP government’s way? Ridings that solidly backed the party in 2023, including all predominantly rural or small-town seats, as well as the seats that include Grande Prairie, Medicine Hat and Fort McMurray.

The all-no seats? Most of them were in Edmonton, some in inner-city Calgary and its northeast, as well as St. Albert — a seat which has gone NDP in the last three elections — and Banff-Kananaskis, which has swung back and forth between UCP and NDP.
Swing ridings?
While a majority of ridings in Alberta went either solidly yes or solidly no, that still leaves 36 provincial constituencies where voters were choosier about how they marked their referendum ballots.
Which seats were running hot and cold on Smith’s plea for referendum support, and might wind up being hotly contested in next year’s election?

Of Calgary’s 26 ridings, 18 of them delivered a mixed yes-and-no verdict on the referendum questions. That includes a handful of NDP-held seats — as well as all the UCP-held seats in the province's largest city.

Calgary has become swing city in Alberta provincial politics, and offered the greatest mix of yes and no verdicts on the premier's referendum questions, compared to the solidly no-leaning Edmonton and yes-leaning other areas of the province. (CBC)
A few suburban Edmonton constituencies broke up the capital’s preference for no with yes majorities on Question 5.

Most of the ridings that surround Edmonton — known politically as the doughnut — swung between yes and no, including NDP-held Sherwood Park, as well as UCP-controlled Spruce Grove-Stony Plain, Strathcona-Sherwood Park, Morinville-St. Albert and Leduc-Beaumont.
Lethbridge’s two seats were a mixed bag too, as they have been politically in the last few elections.

Voters in Alberta’s other two cities of around 100,000 people — Red Deer and rapidly growing Airdrie — have been more consistently UCP in recent votes. But in all four of those cities’ ridings, voters defied Smith’s bid for a clean sweep by voting against Question 8 (and Question 9, in Airdrie-Cochrane).
Calgary-Shaw went orange, but…
Nenshi’s NDP managed to take away a formerly deep-blue suburban seat in September, in the Calgary-Shaw byelection.
The much-watched riding voted yes to all immigration questions last week, but no to all constitutional questions.
Newly elected Calgary-Shaw MLA Kyle Campbell, left, celebrates his byelection victory with NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi. (CBC News)
That more closely resembles voting patterns in other UCP ridings like Calgary-Peigan, Calgary-South East and Calgary-Hays.

However, it’s striking which seat featured a voting result more similar to NDP-held districts: Calgary-West, which voted yes to Question 5 on citizenship markers, but no to the rest. That seat has been held by Deputy Premier Mike Ellis since 2015.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

articles.title: Winnipegger facing extradition over COVID relief fraud, money laundering allegations
articles.summary: A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

image.caption: Ajay Singh of Winnipeg is facing extradition to the U.S. on allegations he was involved in a scheme to defraud a COVID-19 relief program in that country. (Realtor.ca)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Ajay Singh, 46, used fake payroll numbers for forgivable loans through pandemic-era program, U.S. says

Ajay Singh, a 46-year-old Canadian citizen, was arrested last December on allegations he was part of a bank fraud and money laundering scheme to get funds meant to help small businesses pay workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

U.S. officials accused Singh of using inflated or fake payroll numbers to successfully apply for more than $11.5 million US in forgivable loans, according to an extradition request submitted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin.
The lender, Wells Fargo, was able to recover most of the money, but more than $600,000 US was unaccounted for, the document said.
The request did not mention any specific charges Singh — also known as Ajay Singh Kalkat — would face in the U.S. A final decision on whether he should be extradited is pending.

The man had asked courts to stop the proceedings, arguing Canadian authorities violated his Charter rights by issuing an arrest warrant without knowing what he would be charged with. A Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge dismissed that application in September.
The extradition request "contained detailed descriptions of the conduct underlying these allegations, including the names of witnesses and documents," Justice Ami Kotler wrote in the decision.

"This does not mean that Mr. Singh is not entitled to know what charges he is facing in the United States," Kotler said. "But the failure to identify these charges in the warrant application did not, in my view, represent a violation of Mr. Singh's [Charter] rights."

items: 3rd person charged in alleged $11M scheme to defraud Ontario COVID-19 relief fund

blocks.text: The U.S. extradition request said Singh applied to the federal COVID Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) 19 times through three Wisconsin-based companies between 2020 and 2021: Aikam Logistics, AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC and AK Hunt Ltd.
Four of the applications were approved, the document said.

Trucking company Aikam Logistics was granted a $301,882 US loan in 2020 for payroll purposes, with Singh submitting documents that said it had 10 employees. U.S. authorities allege only about $5,000 US appeared to have been spent on items that could possibly be business related.
A year later, Singh submitted another loan application for Aikam, with documents saying the company had 97 employees, the extradition request said. Aikam received a loan for $997,000 US.
Some companies 'existed only on paper,' officials say
Officials pointed to inconsistencies in the number of employees Singh reported to have in 2020 compared with 2021.
The U.S. document also contains allegations the two other companies owned by Singh "existed only on paper in that they did not pay employees or earn revenue."
AK Hunt received a $301,882 US loan based on an application saying it had nine employees in 2020.
AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC. received a $9,975,000 US loan in 2021. The application said the company had 497 employees.
The documents say a witness would be able to testify in court that the office listed as the address for AK Hunt Capital Finance was not large enough to host that many employees.
The witness could say Singh was renting the space for about half a year, paying $450 US a month, officials said.

items: Ex-bureaucrat accused of embezzling COVID-19 funds from Ontario government now facing criminal charges

blocks.text: Wells Fargo began closing business accounts linked to those companies after approving the $9.9-million US loan in March 2021. The document said several identical applications had previously been rejected.
The document said Singh sent a letter to the bank agreeing to reverse the last loan in April 2021 after being interviewed by a Wells Fargo investigator.
"It has come to my attention that the PPP funds should not be used for the purposes I intended," the letter said.
Singh did not address the other loans that were approved, U.S. officials said.
Thousands spent on jewelry, document says

The extradition request said an Internal Revenue Service investigator would be able to give testimony about several transactions that took place after each of the loans was granted, including transfers to broker and personal accounts in multiple banks, as well as cashier cheque purchases.
The investigator had also traced about $15,000 US of the money in jewelry purchases for Singh's wife, the document said.
Kotler said in the September decision the allegations outlined in the U.S. request would have carried a maximum jail sentence of 14 years under Canada's Criminal Code.
An RCMP officer said in an affidavit it was in the public interest to issue the arrest warrant.
Singh was granted bail under several conditions in December, including that he surrender his passport to police.
He was also barred from having sole authority for financial transactions or loans as part of his employment.
The inspector general for the U.S. Small Business Administration estimated more than $200 billion US in COVID-19 aid was potentially fraudulent, including $64 billion US in PPP loan funds.
CBC News tried to contact Singh, but he was not immediately available.
The United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin declined to comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Arturo Chang is a reporter with CBC Manitoba. Before that, he worked for CBC P.E.I. and BNN Bloomberg. You can reach him at arturo.chang@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Malacañang: Nothing wrong with budget insertions as long as used properly
articles.summary: Malacañang responded to a watchdog's finding that Ilocos Norte 1st district had the highest public work insertions in the proposed 2027 budget.

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 5:59pm

Malacañang on Tuesday said that budget “insertions” only become problematic if they go into politicians' pockets, after a watchdog found that Ilocos Norte 1st district had the highest insertions for public works projects in the proposed House General Appropriations Bill (GAB), amounting to P4.37 billion.
The district is represented by President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.'s son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos.

“Kung ang mga proyekto naman ng isang congressman ay maayos at ang pondong ilalaan dito ay magagamit nang tama, sino ba naman ang dapat na humadlang kung ang pondong ito ay sasapat naman para mapaganda ang isang distrito?” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing in Cagayan de Oro City when asked to comment on the People's Budget Coalition's report.
(If a congressman’s projects are justifiable and the allocated funds for such would be properly used to improve the district, then why should we stand in the way?)
“Mahirap po kasi na kumukuha ng pondo, ‘yun pala hindi naman nagagamit sa distrito,” she added.
(What’s problematic is when funds are given only for them not to be used for the district.)
The Palace official said she is not specifically referring to the younger Marcos, but all congressmen in general.
She stressed that there are no problems with such insertions as long as they are used for the welfare of the constituents.

“Kahit sino pang congressman 'yan, kung ang pondo na nailaan sa kanyang distrito ay tama ang paggamit---walang ghost projects, walang substandard na mga materials na ginamit sa mga proyekto---hindi po ito po magkakaroon ng problema,” Castro said.
(Regardless of who the congressman is, as long as the funds allocated to their district are used properly—with no ghost projects and no substandard materials—there shouldn’t be any problem.)
“Dahil ang insertion ay hindi po ito generally masama. Nagiging masama lang ang insertion kung ang pera ay i-insert sa bulsa ng pulitiko. ‘Yun ang masama,” she added.
(An insertion is not inherently bad. It only becomes problematic when the funds are inserted into a politician’s own pocket. That is what’s wrong.)
The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) earlier said it found "red flags" amounting to over P1 trillion in allocations in the proposed P7.2 trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.
These reportedly covered various types of “pork” or discretionary funds under the House-approved GAB

“Lampas P1 trilyong red flags ang nakita namin sa 2027 budget—P210 billion sa soft pork sa anyo ng patronage-driven ayuda, P695 billion sa hard pork, which is politicized infrastructure, and P112 billion po sa shadow pork o ‘yung unprogrammed appropriations,” PBC co-convenor AJ Montesa said in a budget briefing at the Senate on Monday.

(We identified over P1 trillion worth of ‘red flags’ under the 2027 budget—P210 billion of which was ‘soft pork’ in the form of patronage-driven financial assistance; P695 billion in ‘hard pork,’ which consists of politicized infrastructure projects; and P112 billion in ‘shadow pork,’ or unprogrammed appropriations.)

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, in response, said that Congress could make adjustments in the proposed budget with a valid basis. Regardless, he said the Senate would assess if such amendments made by the House were necessary. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Serbia’s student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people take to the streets across the country to celebrate after Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat late on October 25 in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful…

blocks.text: BELGRADE, Serbia – By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday’s election on October 25, Serbia’s student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing — something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.

But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.

The students’ victory “is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centered on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging,” Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday, October 26.

The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024, and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centered on institutional overhauls.

It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia’s former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia’s accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.

Prominent figures include the head of the students’ candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
“(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia’s culture; we will just have to see if it lasts,” said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
“We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system.”
Under Serbia’s constitution, the students’ candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.

Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require “detoxification” after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
In Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.

“We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector,” Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia’s four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.

“I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing — someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms,” said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement. – Rappler.com
